problem:
The function $g(x)$ is continuous over $x\in [2,7].$ Some values of $g(x)$ are given in the table below. 

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g(x)$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $-3$ | $1$ | $0$ | $2$ |

What is the smallest possible number of solutions to the equation $g(x)=-1?$

feedback.problem:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous over $x\in [2,7].$ Some values of $f(x)$ are given in the table below. 

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $1$ | $4$ | $0$ |

What is the smallest possible number of solutions to the equation $f(x)=2?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $f$ is a continuous function on $[2,7]$, we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of $[2,7].$

We will go through each subinterval of $[2,7]$ and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation $f(x)=2$ on this interval.

- On the subinterval $[2,3],$ we have $f(2)=3$ and $f(3)=1.$ Since $2\in [1,3],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=2$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[3,6],$ we have $f(3)=1$ and $f(6)=4.$ Since $2\in [1,4],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=2$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[6,7],$ we have $f(6)=4$ and $f(7)=0.$ Since $2\in [0,4],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $f(x)=2$ on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to $f(x)=2$ on the subintervals $[2,3],$ $[3,6]$ and $[6,7].$  Therefore, $f(x)=2$ has at least three solutions.
